content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Describe the stages of the cell cycle
Understand how the cell cycle is controlled
Explain how uncontrolled cell division leads to cancer
is the series of events that take place in a cell from one division to the next. Cells don't spend all their time dividing - in fact, most of a cell's life is spent in a phase called
Understanding the cell cycle is crucial for understanding growth, development, and diseases like cancer.
The cell cycle consists of two main phases:
- The cell grows and prepares for division (approximately 90% of the cycle)
- The cell divides (approximately 10% of the cycle)

content.text: Interphase is often mistakenly called a "resting phase," but the cell is actually very active during this time. Interphase is divided into three sub-phases:
Normal cell activities occur (protein synthesis, etc.)
Cell produces proteins needed for DNA replication
Cell checks if it's ready to replicate DNA
Variable (hours to years, depending on cell type)
Each chromosome is copied to form two sister chromatids
After S phase, each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
Proteins needed for mitosis are produced
Cell checks that DNA has replicated correctly
(See previous lesson on Mitosis for details)
Some cells leave the cell cycle and enter a resting state called
Cells are metabolically active but not preparing to divide
Some cells can re-enter the cycle if stimulated (e.g., liver cells)
Some cells remain in G0 permanently (e.g., nerve cells, muscle cells)

The cell cycle is controlled by:
- Proteins whose levels rise and fall during the cycle
- Enzymes that control progression through checkpoints
- Genes that slow down cell division (e.g., p53)
When the Cell Cycle Goes Wrong: Cancer
occurs when the normal controls on the cell cycle fail.
Checkpoints fail to stop damaged cells dividing
(cancer) can spread to other parts of the body (metastasis)

content.text: Mutations in genes controlling the cell cycle can be caused by:
is a crucial tumour suppressor gene:
Can stop the cell cycle to allow DNA repair
Can trigger cell death (apoptosis) if damage is too severe
Mutated in over 50% of human cancers
Many cancer treatments target the cell cycle:
- Drugs that stop cells dividing (often target S or M phase)
- Damages DNA, triggering checkpoints and cell death
- Block specific proteins involved in cell cycle control
Understanding the cell cycle helps in:
Growing stem cells for medical treatments
Understanding how cells decide to divide or differentiate
